title: Experiments as explanations
description: A full-feature sample imported pathway: controlled comparisons, optional observation checks, first transfer and delayed independent retrieval.
objective: Investigate how one controlled variable affects a measurable outcome and recognize confounders.

skills.title: Change one variable
skills.label: Lesson 01
skills.kicker: What did the experiment actually test?
skills.pattern: A controlled comparison changes one focal variable while holding relevant alternatives as stable as possible.
pair: Matched seedlings, with equal water and soil, receive six hours of light daily.
Matched seedlings, with equal water and soil, receive eight hours of light daily.
skills.delta: Both examples concern matched seedlings receiving light each day, with water and soil explicitly held equal. Only the daily light exposure changes, from six to eight hours. To attribute a later growth difference to light, a real experiment would also hold watering, soil and other relevant conditions comparable.
anatomy: Identify the outcome that will be measured: growth.
Find the only deliberately changed condition: hours of light.
Check other conditions, such as watering and soil, are comparable across groups.
Compare measured growth and consider replication before claiming causality.
skills.sketch:
GROUP A: matched seedlings + 6 hours of light/day
GROUP B: matched seedlings + 8 hours of light/day
CHANGE: daily light exposure (6 → 8 hours)
MEASURE: subsequent growth
HELD EQUAL: water and soil
ALSO CONTROL IN A REAL TEST: temperature and starting condition
skills.trap: A difference in outcome cannot automatically be assigned to the focal variable if other important conditions also change.
skills.transfer: Ask whether the groups differ in more than one relevant way.

questions.prompt: A researcher tests sunlight's effect on plant height. What is the manipulated variable?
options: Plant height
Hours of sunlight
Final leaf count
Growth rate
questions.explanation: Hours of sunlight are deliberately changed; plant growth is measured.
questions.tip: Which factor does the investigator control?

questions.prompt: Which factor should be held comparable when testing sunlight?
options: Water provided
Hours of sunlight
Growth difference
Measured height
questions.explanation: Water is a potential confounder and should stay comparable.
questions.tip: What else could change plant growth?

questions.prompt: Two plant groups receive different light and different soil. What is the main problem?
options: Both plants grew
More than one relevant condition changed
There were two groups
Growth was measured
questions.explanation: Different soil and light make it harder to isolate which factor caused any growth difference.

questions.prompt: If the groups differ only in light exposure and show different growth, what is the strongest conclusion?
options: Light is certainly the only cause of growth
The result supports an effect of light under these conditions
The result proves all plants react identically
The difference must be random
questions.explanation: A controlled comparison supports the light hypothesis, while scope and replication still matter.
questions.tip: Do not make a conclusion broader than the test.

stable.prompt: Across the two descriptions, which relationship is held constant?
options: The light exposure is always six hours.
Matched seedlings receive a daily light treatment.
Both groups have already grown the same amount.
stable.explanation: Both examples describe matched seedlings receiving daily light; neither says the measured growth is already equal.

changed.prompt: What single feature of the comparison changes?
options: The species of the plants.
The amount of water given to seedlings.
The hours of light per day, from six to eight.
changed.explanation: Only light exposure differs in the opening pair; soil and water have not been changed in those descriptions.

practice.prompt: A team tests whether salt changes how quickly ice melts. Which design changes only the focal variable?
options: Equal ice cubes at the same temperature; only salt amount differs.
Different ice sizes, salt amounts and room temperatures.
Equal salt amounts but different ice sizes.
One ice cube is measured and the other is not.
practice.explanation: Matching cube size and temperature while varying salt isolates the salt condition more clearly.

practice.prompt: Two identical paper airplanes use different wing angles, but one is thrown much harder. Why is the comparison weak?
options: Paper airplanes cannot be tested.
Distance cannot be measured.
Throwing force changed along with wing angle.
The airplanes have wings.
practice.explanation: Throwing force is a second relevant change, so distance differences cannot be isolated to wing angle.
practice.tip: Count the relevant conditions that changed.

practice.prompt: A light experiment changes bulb color and measures moth visits. What is the dependent variable?
options: Bulb color
Number of moth visits
The experimenter's hypothesis
The lamp label
practice.explanation: Moth visits are the measured outcome; bulb color is the manipulated variable.
practice.tip: Separate what is changed from what is measured.

practice.prompt: Replicated trials show a controlled temperature difference is associated with faster germination. Which conclusion is appropriately scoped?
options: Temperature controls every aspect of every seed.
The tested temperature difference affected germination under these conditions.
No other variable can ever matter.
Every plant species must respond identically.
practice.explanation: The result supports a qualified conclusion about the tested conditions without claiming universality.
practice.tip: Keep the claim no broader than the design and observations.

retest.prompt: Two matched yeast cultures differ only in temperature: 24°C versus 30°C. Which inference is justified if they grow at different rates?
options: Temperature is proved to be the sole cause in every culture.
Both temperature and nutrient amount were deliberately changed.
The result supports a temperature effect under these conditions, pending replication.
The result cannot be used because temperatures differ.
retest.explanation: A controlled temperature difference supports a qualified causal hypothesis, but replication and alternative explanations still matter.
retest.tip: Distinguish evidence under tested conditions from universal proof.

retest.prompt: You want to test whether fertilizer type changes root length. Which design most clearly isolates fertilizer type?
options: Same seed variety, water and light; only fertilizer type differs.
Different seed varieties and fertilizers; equal water.
Same fertilizer; different sunlight and soil.
Different fertilizer, water and temperatures for each group.
retest.explanation: Matched conditions isolate fertilizer type as the focal manipulated factor.
retest.tip: Look for the comparison with the fewest relevant simultaneous changes.

retest.prompt: A student claims a new study technique caused better test scores. Both study method and daily sleep changed. What is the main problem?
options: Test scores should never be measured.
Sleep cannot influence attention.
A change in technique is never measurable.
Two relevant factors changed, so the result cannot isolate the technique effect.
retest.explanation: Changing sleep and study method together introduces a potential confounder.
retest.tip: Check whether a competing cause also varies.

retest.prompt: An experiment compares identical containers with the same soil and water, varying only seed depth. What is the dependent variable if investigators measure days until sprouting?
options: Seed depth
Days until sprouting
Container type
Amount of water
retest.explanation: Days until sprouting is the measured outcome; seed depth is the deliberately changed factor.
retest.tip: Separate what is manipulated from what is measured.
